etymology: From the Saxon haeft, a handle, from habban, to have or hold — that part of a tool or weapon which the hand takes. The same root gives the German Heft and stands behind our have.
biblical_def: The haft is the handle of a blade, and it occurs once, in a scene of deliberate and gruesome detail. Ehud, the left-handed judge, has made himself a two-edged dagger of a cubit length and hidden it on his right thigh where no guard would search; he draws it with the wrong hand and drives it into Eglon king of Moab: “And the haft also went in after the blade; and the fat closed upon the blade, so that he could not draw the dagger out of his belly” (Jdg 3:22). The whole weapon disappeared — not merely the edge but the handle, so that Ehud left it inside and went out, locking the doors behind him. The narrator is not being sensational for its own sake. The book of Judges records Israel’s deliverances in their actual grimness, and this one is granted through a man with a disability turned to advantage, a concealed weapon, and eighteen years of tribute-paying patience. Scripture does not romanticise its deliverers, and the reader who wants his heroes clean will find Judges intolerable. That is a mercy, not a defect. A book that told only of blameless saints would have nothing to say to the actual church, and the God of Judges is repeatedly shown raising up flawed and unlikely men because Israel cried unto Him, not because they deserved better.
webster_summary: The handle of a knife, dagger, or tool — the part taken by the hand, as distinguished from the blade.
webster_full: HAFT, n. A handle; that part of an instrument which is taken into the hand.
From the Saxon haeft, a handle, from habban, to have, to hold.
Distinguished from the blade, edge, or head of the instrument.
HAFT, v.t. To set in a haft; to furnish with a handle.
Jdg 3:22: the haft went in after the blade, so that the dagger could not be drawn out.
scriptures: Jdg 3:21
And Ehud put forth his left hand, and took the dagger from his right thigh, and thrust it into his belly:
Jdg 3:22
And the haft also went in after the blade; and the fat closed upon the blade, so that he could not draw the dagger out of his belly; and the dirt came out.
Jdg 2:16
Nevertheless the LORD raised up judges, which delivered them out of the hand of those that spoiled them.
Jdg 3:15

But when the children of Israel cried unto the LORD, the LORD raised them up a deliverer, Ehud the son of Gera, a Benjamite, a man lefthanded : and by him the children of Israel sent a present unto Eglon the king of Moab.
corruption_summary: The narrative books are sanitised for teaching — their violence trimmed and their deliverers tidied — which quietly substitutes a gallery of moral examples for the God who raises up flawed men.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The abiding distortion is the moral-example method of reading Scripture. Judges is retold for children with the daggers removed, and preached to adults as a series of leadership lessons, so that the question put to the text becomes what should I imitate here? Ask that of Ehud and you get nothing usable. Ask it of Samson, Jephthah, or Gideon and you get less. The book resists the method on purpose. Its refrain is that Israel did evil, was sold into the hand of an oppressor, cried unto the LORD, and the LORD raised up a deliverer — four movements in which the only constant actor is God.

Recover the plain sense: the point of the haft disappearing into Eglon is that the deliverance was real, physical, and unlovely, and that God gave it to a people who had earned eighteen years of servitude. Heb 11 later names Gideon, Barak, Samson, and Jephthah among the faithful without pretending they were admirable in everything, which is exactly how Scripture handles its saints — Noah drunk, Abraham lying, David worse. To sand these accounts down is to lose the doctrine they were written to teach: that salvation comes from outside the sinner, and that God’s choice of instruments is governed by His mercy rather than by their merit.
roots_summary: Saxon haeft, a handle — the part the hand holds; buried with the blade in Eglon’s belly.
roots_lines: Haft — Saxon haeft, a handle, from habban, to hold.
Kin to the German Heft and to English have.
The handle as distinguished from the blade or head.
Jdg 3:22: haft and blade both entered; the weapon was left inside.
Ehud was left-handed and wore the dagger on the right thigh — concealment by exception.
usage: Judges records its deliverances in their real grimness, without tidying the deliverers.
The refrain of the book puts the constancy on God’s side, not the judge’s.
Heb 11 names these men as faithful without pretending they were exemplary throughout.

etymology: From the Saxon helf or hielfe, a handle — specifically the long wooden handle of an axe or hatchet, as distinguished from the haft of a knife.
biblical_def: The helve is the axe-handle, and its single occurrence is the crux of one of the most humane provisions in the law: “As when a man goeth into the wood with his neighbour to hew wood, and his hand fetcheth a stroke with the axe to cut down the tree, and the head slippeth from the helve, and lighteth upon his neighbour, that he die; he shall flee unto one of those cities, and live” (Deu 19:5). Consider how carefully the case is framed. Two neighbours are working together, in ordinary labour, at a lawful task; the man swings honestly; the iron flies off the handle and kills his friend. There is no malice, no negligence stated, nothing anyone would call a crime — and a man is dead, and the avenger of blood is entitled to pursue. The law does not pretend the death did not happen, nor does it hand the axeman over. It builds cities and paves roads to them, so that the slayer may run “lest the avenger of the blood pursue the slayer, while his heart is hot” (Deu 19:6). Two truths are held together that our own age can rarely hold at once: blood guilt is real even when intent is absent, and mercy must be made physically reachable. God did not merely declare the unintentional slayer pardonable; He surveyed the ground and set the cities where a running man could get to them.
webster_summary: The handle of an axe or hatchet; the wooden shaft from which the iron head may slip.
webster_full: HELVE, n. The handle of an axe or hatchet.
From the Saxon helf, hielfe, a handle.
Distinguished from haft, which is properly the handle of a knife or dagger.
HELVE, v.t. To furnish with a helve, as an axe.
Deu 19:5: the head slipping from the helve is the law’s example of death without intent.
scriptures: Deu 19:4
And this is the case of the slayer, which shall flee thither, that he may live: Whoso killeth his neighbour ignorantly , whom he hated not in time past;
Deu 19:5

As when a man goeth into the wood with his neighbour to hew wood, and his hand fetcheth a stroke with the axe to cut down the tree, and the head slippeth from the helve, and lighteth upon his neighbour, that he die; he shall flee unto one of those cities, and live:
Deu 19:6

Lest the avenger of the blood pursue the slayer , while his heart is hot, and overtake him, because the way is long, and slay him; whereas he was not worthy of death, inasmuch as he hated him not in time past.

And the congregation shall deliver the slayer out of the hand of the revenger of blood, and the congregation shall restore him to the city of his refuge, whither he was fled: and he shall abide in it unto the death of the high priest, which was anointed with the holy oil.
corruption_summary: Modern justice tends to collapse into one of two errors — treating absence of intent as absence of harm, or treating harm as proof of malice — where the law of the helve holds real bloodguilt and real mercy together.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption runs both ways, and the law of Deu 19 refutes both. On one side stands the doctrine that intention is everything: if a man did not mean it, nothing has happened that requires anything of him, and to ask more is cruelty. On the other stands the reflex that treats every injury as evidence of wickedness, so that an accident becomes an accusation and no distinction survives between the axe that slipped and the axe that was aimed. Scripture refuses both. It insists that a real death has occurred and that blood defiles the land, and it insists with equal firmness that the man who did not lie in wait shall live. The very existence of the cities of refuge presupposes both halves; a purely innocent man would need no city, and a murderer was to be taken even from the altar.

Recover the plain sense: mercy in Scripture is not a mood but an arrangement. God did not announce that unintentional slayers were forgiven and leave them to argue it out with a hot-hearted avenger on the road. He appointed six cities, three on each side of Jordan, distributed so that no Israelite was impossibly far from one, and the rabbis record that the roads were kept clear and signposted. That is what serious mercy looks like — costly, planned, and reachable. And the refuge had a term set by a death: the slayer returned home at the death of the high priest (Num 35:25), so that even accidental blood was answered by a priestly death and not by a legal fiction.
roots_summary: Saxon helf, an axe-handle — the shaft the head slips from; the law’s chosen picture of death without intent.
roots_lines: Helve — Saxon helf, the handle of an axe.
Distinguished from haft, the handle of a knife or dagger.
Deu 19:5: the head slippeth from the helve and lighteth upon his neighbour.
The case is chosen precisely for its innocence — lawful work, honest stroke.
Num 35:25: the slayer returns home at the death of the high priest.
usage: The law holds both truths: real bloodguilt without intent, and real mercy made reachable.
Deu 19:6 explains the urgency — the avenger’s heart is hot and the way is long.
Refuge ends at a priest’s death, not by a legal fiction.

etymology: From the Latin malleus, a hammer, through the Old French mail — the same root as mallet and malleable. A maul is a heavy hammer or war-club, a weapon of crushing rather than cutting.
biblical_def: Solomon names three weapons in a single verse and assigns all of them to one sin: “A man that beareth false witness against his neighbour is a maul, and a sword, and a sharp arrow” (Pro 25:18). The three are chosen with care, for they cover every range and every kind of wound. The maul crushes at close quarters, the sword cuts at arm’s length, and the sharp arrow strikes a man who never saw the archer. So the false witness destroys near and far, openly and invisibly, and the proverb does not say he is like these things — it says he is a maul, and a sword, and a sharp arrow. The man is the weapon. This sits within the ninth commandment’s wide reach, which Scripture applies not only to formal perjury but to the whole traffic of the tongue: talebearing, whispering, backbiting, and the report passed on without inquiry. Solomon elsewhere sets the alternative plainly: “There is that speaketh like the piercings of a sword: but the tongue of the wise is health” (Pro 12:18). Two tongues, two effects, and no neutral ground. What is said of a neighbour either wounds him or heals him, and the speaker is choosing his instrument every time he opens his mouth.
webster_summary: A heavy hammer or war-club used for crushing; in Proverbs, one of three weapons the false witness is said to be.
webster_full: MAUL, n. A heavy wooden hammer; a beetle; anciently, a club or mace used in war.
From the Latin malleus, a hammer; Old French mail.
Of the same family as mallet, malleable, and malleus.
MAUL, v.t. To beat and bruise with a heavy instrument; to wound grossly.
Pro 25:18 sets it with the sword and the arrow as the arms of a false witness.
scriptures: A man that beareth false witness against his neighbour is a maul, and a sword, and a sharp arrow.
Thou shalt not bear false witness against thy neighbour.
There is that speaketh like the piercings of a sword: but the tongue of the wise is health.
Pro 18:8
The words of a talebearer are as wounds, and they go down into the innermost parts of the belly.
corruption_summary: The ninth commandment is widely narrowed to courtroom perjury, leaving gossip, the unverified report, and the passed-on rumour untouched — though these are precisely the maul’s ordinary work.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is the shrinking of the ninth commandment to a legal technicality. Most people, asked whether they have borne false witness, think of a witness box and answer no with a clear conscience. Solomon has a wider field in view, and so does the whole of Scripture: thou shalt not go up and down as a talebearer among thy people; the words of a talebearer are as wounds, and they go down into the innermost parts of the belly (Pro 18:8); backbiters are listed among those given over in Rom 1. The commandment governs everything said against a neighbour, and the modern machinery for saying it — the forwarded message, the anonymous account, the story repeated because it is interesting — has enlarged the maul’s reach beyond anything Solomon saw.

Recover the plain sense: the test is not merely is it true but is it mine to say, to this person, for this reason. A true report circulated to wound is still a weapon, and Pro 18:8 warns that such words are received eagerly and lodge deep, which is why retraction never undoes them. Set against it the alternative Solomon names: the tongue of the wise is health. That is the striking thing about Pro 12:18 — speech is never inert. It is either piercing or healing, maul or medicine, and the same mouth is capable of both. The ninth commandment does not merely forbid the weapon; it puts a physician’s instrument in your hand instead.
roots_summary: Latin malleus, a hammer — a crushing club; one of the three weapons Solomon says a false witness is.
roots_lines: Maul — Latin malleus, a hammer; Old French mail.
Kin to mallet and malleable.
A crushing weapon, used at close quarters, unlike the sword or arrow.
Pro 25:18 covers every range: maul near, sword at arm’s length, arrow unseen.
The proverb does not say like a maul — the man is the weapon.
usage: Three weapons, one sin: false witness wounds near, far, and invisibly.
The ninth commandment reaches talebearing and backbiting, not only perjury.
Pro 12:18 gives the alternative — the tongue of the wise is health.

etymology: From the Old French lancette, a little lance, diminutive of lance — Latin lancea. A small, sharp, double-edged blade; the surgeon’s instrument for opening a vein, and hence any small piercing blade.
biblical_def: The word stands at the heart of Carmel: the prophets of Baal, having called on their god from morning until noon with no answer, “cried aloud, and cut themselves after their manner with knives and lancets, till the blood gushed out upon them” (1Ki 18:28). Every feature of false religion is on display in that one verse. There is volume — they cried aloud. There is duration — from morning until the time of the evening sacrifice. There is technique — after their manner, an established liturgy of self-wounding. And there is escalation: when nothing happens, the answer is always to do more of it, harder, bloodier. What there is not, at any point, is a word from Baal, “for there was no voice, nor any that answered” (1Ki 18:26). Set beside this the God of Israel, whose prophet prays a prayer of some sixty words at the appointed hour of sacrifice, and the fire falls. Israel had been expressly forbidden this practice: “Ye are the children of the LORD your God: ye shall not cut yourselves” (Deu 14:1) — and note the ground of the prohibition. It is not that self-wounding is unseemly but that they are children. Sons do not have to bleed to get their Father’s attention.
webster_summary: Small sharp double-edged blades, as of a surgeon; the instruments with which the prophets of Baal gashed themselves on Carmel.
webster_full: LANCET, n. A small pointed surgical instrument, sharp on both edges, used in opening veins and tumours.
From the Old French lancette, a little lance; Latin lancea.
Any small piercing blade; in architecture, a narrow pointed window or arch.
1Ki 18:28: the prophets of Baal cut themselves with knives and lancets.
Such self-laceration was expressly forbidden to Israel (Lev 19:28; Deu 14:1).
scriptures: And they took the bullock which was given them, and they dressed it, and called on the name of Baal from morning even until noon, saying, O Baal, hear us. But there was no voice, nor any that answered. And they leaped upon the altar which was made.
And they cried aloud , and cut themselves after their manner with knives and lancets, till the blood gushed out upon them.
And it came to pass, when midday was past, and they prophesied until the time of the offering of the evening sacrifice, that there was neither voice, nor any to answer, nor any that regarded.
Deu 14:1
Ye are the children of the LORD your God: ye shall not cut yourselves, nor make any baldness between your eyes for the dead.
corruption_summary: Wherever acceptance with God is thought to depend on the intensity of the worshipper’s exertion — louder, longer, costlier, more painful — Carmel’s liturgy is being repeated with different instruments.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is worship measured by exertion. Baal’s prophets operated on a perfectly coherent principle: the god is reluctant, the worshipper must overcome that reluctance, and the currency of persuasion is intensity — volume, endurance, and finally blood. The instruments have changed; the principle is endemic. It appears in penance and self-flagellation, in the notion that a prayer must reach a certain pitch or length to be heard, in the sense that a service has failed unless the emotion ran high, and in the quiet conviction of many sincere believers that God attends to them in proportion to their fervour. All of it assumes a God who must be moved, and all of it puts the worshipper at the centre of the transaction.

Recover the plain sense: Elijah prayed briefly, at the hour God had already appointed for sacrifice, and asked expressly that the people might know that thou hast turned their heart back again — giving even their repentance to God. The fire fell on a soaked altar, in the evening, at the time of the offering, and it consumed the sacrifice rather than the prophet. That is the gospel pattern: the fire falls on the substitute. Deu 14:1 supplies the doctrine underneath — ye are the children of the LORD your God, therefore ye shall not cut yourselves. Sonship is the reason self-wounding is forbidden. A child who must bleed to be noticed has not understood his adoption.
roots_summary: Old French lancette, a little lance — a small piercing blade; the tool of Baal’s liturgy on Carmel.
roots_lines: Lancets — Old French lancette, diminutive of lance; Latin lancea.
A small double-edged blade, properly the surgeon’s vein-opener.
1Ki 18:28: used after their manner — an established liturgy of self-wounding.
Forbidden to Israel on the ground of sonship (Deu 14:1).
The contrast at Carmel is exertion against appointment: hours of blood, then a short prayer and fire.
usage: False religion escalates when unanswered; it has no category but more.
Elijah prays at the appointed hour of sacrifice, and the fire consumes the substitute.
Deu 14:1 forbids self-cutting because Israel are children, not suppliants.

etymology: The older past tense of strike, from the Saxon strican. In Act 27:17 the phrase strake sail is the seaman’s idiom for striking — that is, lowering — the sail, the same sense in which a ship strikes her colours.
biblical_def: “Which when they had taken up, they used helps, undergirding the ship; and, fearing lest they should fall into the quicksands, strake sail, and so were driven” (Act 27:17). The verse is the turning point of the greatest sea narrative in Scripture. Caught by the tempestuous wind Euroclydon (Act 27:14), the crew do everything seamanship allows: they take up the boat, they frap the hull with cables to keep her from breaking apart, and then they lower the sail — the last resort, the surrender of all steering — and are driven. To strike sail is to stop trying to make headway and let the storm carry you. For fourteen days they drift, and the narrative records that all hope was taken away. It is precisely there, when the ship is being driven and every competence has been exhausted, that Paul stands forth and says, “be of good cheer: for I believe God, that it shall be even as it was told me” (Act 27:25). Two things sit together in this chapter and must not be separated. Every measure of ordinary seamanship is used, energetically and to the last; and the deliverance, when it comes, is by promise and not by seamanship. God had told Paul that not a soul would be lost, and not a soul was — and they still had to keep the sailors from escaping in the boat.
webster_summary: The older past tense of strike; in the phrase strake sail, to lower the sail in a storm, surrendering headway and letting the ship be driven.
webster_full: STRIKE, v.t. To lower; to let down; as, to strike sail, or to strike a flag.
STRAKE, the old past tense of strike; Saxon strican.
To strike sail is to lower the sails, in submission, in salute, or in stress of weather.
Figuratively, to yield; to abate pretensions; to acknowledge a superior.
Act 27:17: they strake sail, and so were driven before the tempest.
scriptures: But not long after there arose against it a tempestuous wind, called Euroclydon.
Which when they had taken up, they used helps, undergirding the ship; and, fearing lest they should fall into the quicksands, strake sail, and so were driven.
And when neither sun nor stars in many days appeared, and no small tempest lay on us, all hope that we should be saved was then taken away.
Wherefore, sirs, be of good cheer: for I believe God, that it shall be even as it was told me.
corruption_summary: Providence is habitually set against effort, so that trusting God is imagined to mean ceasing to work — while Acts 27 shows a crew frapping the hull and cutting away the boat inside an absolute divine promise.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is the false alternative between faith and means. It takes two forms, and Acts 27 rebukes both. The first says that if God has promised, effort is superfluous — let go, let God, and stop striving. The second says that since the sea is indifferent and the ship is real, seamanship is all there is, and prayer is a gesture. Luke, who was aboard, records neither. He records cables under the hull, tackling thrown overboard, soundings taken, four anchors cast out of the stern, and a wheat cargo jettisoned — alongside an angel of God standing by Paul in the night with an unconditional word: God hath given thee all them that sail with thee.

Recover the plain sense: the sharpest illustration is Act 27:31. God had promised that not one life would be lost, and when the sailors tried to flee in the boat Paul said, Except these abide in the ship, ye cannot be saved — and the soldiers cut the ropes and let her fall off. The promise was certain and the means were necessary, and Paul saw no contradiction whatever between them. God ordains ends and means together, which is why the doctrine of providence has never in Reformed hands produced fatalism. Strike sail when seamanship is exhausted; keep sounding, keep praying, keep the crew aboard; and be of good cheer on the ground Paul names — not because the storm looks survivable, but for I believe God.
roots_summary: Saxon strican, the old past tense of strike — to lower sail; the surrender of headway inside an unbroken promise.
roots_lines: Strake — the older past tense of strike; Saxon strican.
To strike sail is the seaman’s idiom for lowering the sail.
The same idiom gives striking a flag or colours — a token of submission.
Act 27:17: the last resort, after undergirding the ship with helps.
Act 27:20: neither sun nor stars appeared for many days, and all hope was taken away.
usage: To strike sail is to give up headway and be driven — the end of seamanship.
Act 27:31: the promise was absolute and the means were still necessary.
Paul’s ground of cheer is not the weather but I believe God.

etymology: From the Old French boce, a swelling or protuberance. A boss is the raised knob at the centre of a shield, thickened to take the blow and to turn a weapon aside; hence any rounded projection in metalwork or architecture.
biblical_def: The word occurs once, in Eliphaz’s description of the wicked man charging God: “He runneth upon him, even on his neck, upon the thick bosses of his bucklers” (Job 15:26). The image is of a warrior who lowers his head, presents the reinforced centre of his shield, and runs full at his opponent — the ancient equivalent of a charge behind a raised guard. And the opponent is God: the previous verse says “he stretcheth out his hand against God, and strengtheneth himself against the Almighty” (Job 15:25). The picture is magnificently absurd, and is meant to be. A man gathers his defences, thickens his shield, picks his moment, and charges the Almighty. Eliphaz is a poor comforter and much of his counsel is wrong — God says at the end that Eliphaz has not spoken of Him the thing that is right — but this particular image is sound, and Scripture uses the same picture elsewhere for the futility of rebellion. Note the ironic detail: the wicked man’s thick bosses are precisely his strength, the reinforced part, the place he trusts. Men do not run at God behind their weakness. They run behind whatever they are proudest of, and the thickness of the boss is the measure of the folly.
webster_summary: The raised central knobs of shields, thickened to receive and turn a blow; hence any rounded projection in metal or stone.
webster_full: BOSS, n. A stud or knob; a protuberant ornament of silver, ivory, or other material.
A protuberant part; the raised centre of a shield, or of a buckler.
From the Old French boce, a swelling, a bump.
In architecture, a projecting ornament at the intersection of the ribs of a vault.
Job 15:26: to run upon the thick bosses of a buckler is to charge behind the strongest part of the guard.
scriptures: For he stretcheth out his hand against God, and strengtheneth himself against the Almighty.
He runneth upon him, even on his neck, upon the thick bosses of his bucklers:
Psa 2:4
He that sitteth in the heavens shall laugh: the Lord shall have them in derision.
Isa 45:9
Woe unto him that striveth with his Maker! Let the potsherd strive with the potsherds of the earth. Shall the clay say to him that fashioneth it, What makest thou? or thy work, He hath no hands?
corruption_summary: Rebellion against God is imagined as intellectual courage, the brave man standing against a tyrant — where Scripture pictures a creature charging the Almighty behind the thickest part of his own shield.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is the heroic pose of unbelief. Rebellion presents itself as bravery: the free thinker refusing an imposed authority, the honest doubter who will not pretend, the man who would rather stand alone than kneel. Scripture never grants the posture its dignity. Psa 2 has the kings of the earth setting themselves against the LORD and His Anointed, and the response from heaven is laughter — He that sitteth in the heavens shall laugh (Psa 2:4). Isaiah reduces it further: Woe unto him that striveth with his Maker! Let the potsherd strive with the potsherds of the earth (Isa 45:9). A shard of pottery arguing with the potter. Eliphaz’s picture belongs to the same family — the charge is real, the shield is thick, and the target is the Almighty.

Recover the plain sense: the folly is located precisely in the strength. Men run at God behind their thick bosses — their competence, their intellect, their record, their moral seriousness — and it is the trusted part that makes the charge possible. That is why God so often deals with a man by breaking exactly what he was proudest of. Jacob wrestled and went away with a limp; Paul was struck blind at the height of his zeal; Nebuchadnezzar was reduced to grass at the summit of his empire. The mercy is in the disarming. A man who lays the buckler down is not defeated but delivered, for the God he was charging is the God who receives him.
roots_summary: Old French boce, a swelling — the shield’s reinforced centre; the strong point behind which men charge God.
roots_lines: Bosses — Old French boce, a swelling or protuberance.
The raised knob at a shield’s centre, thickened to take and turn a blow.
In architecture, the carved projection at a vault’s rib-intersection.
Job 15:26: running on God behind the thick bosses of the buckler.
Job 15:25 gives the act: he strengtheneth himself against the Almighty.
usage: Eliphaz is a poor comforter, but this image is sound and Scripture repeats it elsewhere.
Psa 2:4 and Isa 45:9 treat rebellion as absurdity, never as courage.
The folly lies in the strength: men charge God behind what they trust most.

etymology: The Authorized Version’s spelling of brazen, from the Saxon braes, brass — made of brass or copper. The metal of the outer court and of judgment, as gold is the metal of the holy place.
biblical_def: Brasen is the metal of the outer court, and its distribution through the tabernacle is a sermon in itself. Gold is used within the veil, silver in the sockets of redemption, and brass where the fire and the blood are — the brasen altar with “his brasen grate” (Exo 35:16), the brasen rings (Exo 27:4), the laver of brass made “of the lookingglasses of the women assembling” (Exo 38:8). Brass in Scripture is associated with strength that endures fire and therefore with judgment: the heavens over a disobedient people are brass, and the feet of the Son of man are like unto fine brass, as if they burned in a furnace. The metal’s greatest moment is the brasen serpent. Bitten Israel is told to look at a serpent of brass upon a pole, and “if a serpent had bitten any man, when he beheld the serpent of brass, he lived” (Num 21:9) — a cure by looking, not by doing, at an image of the very curse that was killing them. Our Lord claims it: “as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, even so must the Son of man be lifted up” (Joh 3:14). And the sequel is as instructive as the sign. Seven centuries later Hezekiah “brake in pieces the brasen serpent that Moses had made” (2Ki 18:4), because Israel had begun burning incense to it. He called it Nehushtan — a piece of brass.
webster_summary: Made of brass; the metal of the tabernacle’s outer court, of the altar and laver, and of the serpent lifted up in the wilderness.
webster_full: BRASEN, BRAZEN, adj. Made of brass; pertaining to brass.
From the Saxon braes, brass; the AV retains the older spelling.
Impudent; having a front like brass; as, a brazen face — a secondary sense.
In the tabernacle, the metal of the outer court: the altar, the laver, the grate, the pins.
Num 21:9: the serpent of brass lifted upon a pole for the healing of Israel.
scriptures: Exo 27:4
And thou shalt make for it a grate of network of brass; and upon the net shalt thou make four brasen rings in the four corners thereof.
Num 21:9
And Moses made a serpent of brass, and put it upon a pole, and it came to pass, that if a serpent had bitten any man, when he beheld the serpent of brass, he lived.

He removed the high places, and brake the images, and cut down the groves, and brake in pieces the brasen serpent that Moses had made: for unto those days the children of Israel did burn incense to it: and he called it Nehushtan.
Joh 3:14
And as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, even so must the Son of man be lifted up:
corruption_summary: The brasen serpent is the Bible’s own case study in a God-given sign becoming an idol — and Hezekiah’s remedy shows that antiquity and divine origin are no defence once a thing is being worshipped.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is the veneration of the instrument. Nothing in Israel had better credentials than the brasen serpent. It was made at God’s express command, by Moses himself, and thousands had been healed by looking at it — genuine miracle, impeccable pedigree, seven hundred years of history. And Israel burned incense to it, and Hezekiah broke it in pieces and called it Nehushtan, which is to say, a bit of brass. The lesson is unsparing and is aimed straight at the church. A means God has genuinely used will be turned into an object of trust if men are left to themselves, and the better the credentials, the more plausible the idolatry.

Recover the plain sense: apply Hezekiah’s hammer where it belongs. The dictionary rejects the veneration of relics, images, and sacred objects on exactly this ground — if the serpent Moses made at God’s command had to be destroyed, no crucifix, bone, or icon has a better claim. But the principle reaches further than images. A translation, a confession, a hymnody, a preacher, a method of prayer, a revival remembered — each may be a real gift of God and each may be burned incense to. The test is simple: is this thing pointing away from itself to Christ, or has it become the object of the look? Joh 3:14 fixes the serpent’s true meaning forever. It was never to be gazed at as a relic; it was a picture of the Son of man lifted up, and the look that saves goes through it to Him.
roots_summary: Saxon braes, brass — the metal of the outer court and of judgment; the serpent lifted up, and the idol Hezekiah broke.
roots_lines: Brasen — the AV spelling of brazen; Saxon braes, brass.
The metal of the outer court: altar, grate, laver, rings, and pins.
Gold within the veil, silver in the sockets, brass where fire and blood are.
Num 21:9: healing by looking at an image of the curse itself.
2Ki 18:4: Hezekiah brake it in pieces and called it Nehushtan.
usage: The brasen serpent had the best credentials in Israel and still became an idol.
Joh 3:14 fixes its meaning: a type of the Son of man lifted up.
The test of any means: does it point past itself to Christ?

etymology: From the Saxon fetor, from fet, the foot — chains for the feet, as manacles (Latin manus) are chains for the hands. The word names the place it binds.
biblical_def: Fetters bind the feet, and Scripture reserves them for men whose strength or station made them seem unbindable. Samson, the strongest man in Israel, is taken, blinded, and “bound with fetters of brass; and he did grind in the prison house” (Jdg 16:21) — the deliverer grinding at a mill like a beast. Zedekiah, the last king of Judah, sees his sons slain, is blinded, and is bound “with fetters of brass” and carried to Babylon (2Ki 25:7); the last thing he ever saw was his children dying. Manasseh, the worst king Judah produced, is taken among the thorns and bound with fetters (2Ch 33:11) — and that fettering is the only thing that ever brought him to repentance, for in his affliction he besought the LORD and God was intreated of him. Abner’s dirge grieves that a great man died undefended: “Thy hands were not bound, nor thy feet put into fetters” (2Sa 3:34). And the Gadarene demoniac breaks them: he had been “often bound with fetters and chains, and the chains had been plucked asunder by him, and the fetters broken in pieces” (Mar 5:4) — a man no chain could hold, sitting a few verses later clothed and in his right mind at the feet of Jesus. Every use turns on the same irony. The strongest are the ones in fetters, and the only real liberty in any of these accounts is given, not seized.
webster_summary: Chains or shackles for the feet, used to bind prisoners; in Scripture the portion of the strong, the royal, and the possessed.
webster_full: FETTER, n. A chain for the feet; a shackle used to confine the legs of a prisoner.
From the Saxon fetor, from fet, the foot; as manacle from the Latin manus, the hand.
Anything that confines or restrains from motion.
FETTER, v.t. To put chains on the feet; to bind; to restrain.
Frequently of brass in Scripture (Jdg 16:21; 2Ki 25:7).
scriptures: But the Philistines took him, and put out his eyes, and brought him down to Gaza, and bound him with fetters of brass; and he did grind in the prison house.
And they slew the sons of Zedekiah before his eyes, and put out the eyes of Zedekiah, and bound him with fetters of brass, and carried him to Babylon.
Wherefore the LORD brought upon them the captains of the host of the king of Assyria, which took Manasseh among the thorns, and bound him with fetters, and carried him to Babylon.
Mar 5:4
Because that he had been often bound with fetters and chains, and the chains had been plucked asunder by him, and the fetters broken in pieces: neither could any man tame him .
corruption_summary: Freedom is now defined as the absence of restraint, so the men Scripture shows in fetters — and the one man Scripture shows breaking them — are read exactly backwards.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is the identification of liberty with the absence of limits. On that definition the Gadarene demoniac was the freest man in the region: no chain held him, no house contained him, no authority governed him, and he lived beyond every boundary society could impose. Scripture calls his condition possession, and describes him crying night and day among the tombs and cutting himself with stones. Meanwhile Samson, who had every physical liberty and used it to indulge every appetite, ends in literal fetters grinding at a mill — and the text is careful to note that his fall began long before the chains, when he did not know that the LORD was departed from him.

Recover the plain sense: the man who could break every fetter was not free, and Manasseh in fetters was closer to freedom than Manasseh on the throne. That is the pattern the histories keep pressing. He was bound, says the chronicler of the worst king in Judah’s line, and then, when he was in affliction, he besought the LORD his God, and humbled himself greatly. The fetters did what fifty-five years of prosperity had not. And the Gadarene shows the end of the matter: the chains that could not hold him were not needed once he was delivered, and he is found sitting, clothed, in his right mind, at the feet of Jesus, begging to stay with Him. That is liberty — not a man whom nothing can bind, but a man bound to the right Master.
roots_summary: Saxon fetor, from fet, the foot — chains for the feet; the portion of Samson, Zedekiah, Manasseh, and the possessed.
roots_lines: Fetters — Saxon fetor, from fet, the foot.
Answering to manacles, from Latin manus, the hand.
Commonly of brass in the histories (Jdg 16:21; 2Ki 25:7).
2Ch 33:11: Manasseh’s fetters were the occasion of his repentance.
Mar 5:4: the demoniac broke every fetter and was not thereby free.
usage: Scripture puts fetters on the strong and the royal — the unbindable men.
Manasseh’s chains accomplished what fifty-five years of prosperity did not.
The man no chain could hold was possessed; liberty is being bound to the right Master.

etymology: From the Latin bilanx — bis, twice, and lanx, a plate or scale — the two-pan scale. The word is plural in form because the instrument is double: two pans, one truth, and no verdict possible without both.
biblical_def: The balances are Scripture’s standing image of judgment, and the law treats their honesty as a matter of the LORD’s own name: “Just balances, just weights, a just ephah, and a just hin, shall ye have: I am the LORD your God, which brought you out of the land of Egypt” (Lev 19:36). The reason attached is redemption — a people bought out of Egypt do not cheat in the marketplace. Solomon states the matter as strongly as anything in Proverbs: “A false balance is abomination to the LORD: but a just weight is his delight” (Pro 11:1). Note the two words: not merely displeasing but abomination, and not merely acceptable but delight. God takes personal pleasure in an honest shopkeeper. Job, protesting his integrity, asks for the instrument to be used on him: “Let me be weighed in an even balance, that God may know mine integrity” (Job 31:6) — a bold request, and one the book does not condemn. And the image reaches its terrible fulfilment on a wall in Babylon, where a hand wrote three words and Daniel read the second: “TEKEL; Thou art weighed in the balances, and art found wanting” (Dan 5:27). Belshazzar had drunk from the vessels of the temple that night. He was weighed the same night, and slain in it.
webster_summary: A pair of scales for weighing; in Scripture the emblem of just dealing in trade and of God’s judgment of men.
webster_full: BALANCE, n. A pair of scales; an instrument for ascertaining the weight of bodies.
From the Latin bilanx, from bis, twice, and lanx, a plate or dish.
The instrument consists of a beam suspended at its middle with a scale at each end.
Figuratively, the means of estimating or comparing; as, to weigh in the balance.
In Scripture, the emblem of just weight in commerce (Lev 19:36) and of divine judgment (Dan 5:27).
scriptures: Just balances, just weights, a just ephah, and a just hin, shall ye have: I am the LORD your God, which brought you out of the land of Egypt.
Pro 11:1
A false balance is abomination to the LORD: but a just weight is his delight.
Job 31:6
Let me be weighed in an even balance, that God may know mine integrity.
Dan 5:27
TEKEL; Thou art weighed in the balances, and art found wanting.
corruption_summary: Commercial honesty is filed under business ethics rather than worship, though Scripture attaches the just weight directly to God’s name, His delight, and the exodus itself.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is the partition of life into sacred and commercial. Weights and measures feel like a technical matter, properly governed by regulation and competition rather than by piety, and a man may be devout on Sunday and sharp on Monday without ever noticing a contradiction. Scripture makes no such division. Lev 19:36 puts just balances in the same chapter as loving thy neighbour as thyself and reverencing the sanctuary, and it grounds them all in one sentence: I am the LORD your God, which brought you out of the land of Egypt. Redemption is the reason for an honest scale. Pro 11:1 then raises the temperature: a false balance is abomination, a word Scripture reserves for idolatry and the grossest sins, while a just weight is God’s delight.

Recover the plain sense: the balance is where doctrine becomes visible to people who will never hear you preach. Every trade has its equivalent of the thumb on the scale — the padded invoice, the quiet substitution, the disclosed-in-small-print charge, the hour billed and not worked — and each is a small liturgy declaring what its author believes about God. Then let Dan 5:27 do its work. Belshazzar was weighed, and the instrument he was weighed in was the very one the law had commanded him to keep honest. Men who spend a life adjusting the scale should consider that they will one day stand in it, and that the hand which writes on the wall does not require a second opinion.
roots_summary: Latin bilanx, two-panned — the scale; emblem of just trade and of the judgment in which Belshazzar was found wanting.
roots_lines: Balances — Latin bilanx, from bis, twice, and lanx, a pan.
Plural in form because the instrument is double: two pans, one truth.
Lev 19:36 grounds the just weight in the exodus: I am the LORD your God.
Pro 11:1: a false balance is abomination; a just weight is His delight.
Dan 5:27: TEKEL — weighed in the balances, and found wanting.
usage: The law places honest weights beside loving thy neighbour and reverencing the sanctuary.
God is said to take personal delight in a just weight.
Job asks to be weighed; Belshazzar was weighed without asking.

etymology: From the Latin copula, a bond or tie, through the Old French copler — the joining of two things into one. In Exodus it is the technical term for the seam where two sets of tabernacle curtains are joined.
biblical_def: The coupling is a seam, and the Holy Ghost spends an extraordinary number of verses on it. “Thou shalt make loops of blue upon the edge of the one curtain from the selvedge in the coupling” (Exo 26:4); fifty loops answering fifty loops, “that the loops may take hold one of another”; then “fifty taches of gold, and couple the curtains together with the taches: and it shall be one tabernacle” (Exo 26:6). Over the tent of goats’ hair, the same again in brass: “put the taches into the loops, and couple the tent together, that it may be one” (Exo 26:11). The refrain is unmistakable — that it may be one. Ten curtains, and the chapter will not rest until they are a single dwelling. Nothing in the tabernacle was designed by a committee of preference; every loop was counted and every clasp specified, because the house where God met His people had to be one house. The New Testament takes the figure up without apology: the church is a building fitly framed together, growing unto an holy temple in the Lord, “from whom the whole body fitly joined together and compacted by that which every joint supplieth” (Eph 4:16). The couplings are the joints, and the strength of the whole is measured at the seams — which is exactly where a fabric tears.
webster_summary: The seam or joining where two curtains are united; that which couples or fastens things together into one.
webster_full: COUPLING, n. That which couples or connects; the joining of two things.
The place or seam where two breadths are united.
From the Latin copula, a band or tie; Old French copler, to join.
In the tabernacle, the seam at which the sets of curtains were joined by loops and taches (Exo 26:4–6).
In mechanics, the contrivance connecting one part or carriage with another.
scriptures: Exo 26:4

And thou shalt make loops of blue upon the edge of the one curtain from the selvedge in the coupling; and likewise shalt thou make in the uttermost edge of another curtain, in the coupling of the second.
Exo 26:6
And thou shalt make fifty taches of gold, and couple the curtains together with the taches: and it shall be one tabernacle.
And thou shalt make fifty taches of brass, and put the taches into the loops, and couple the tent together, that it may be one.
Eph 4:16

From whom the whole body fitly joined together and compacted by that which every joint supplieth, according to the effectual working in the measure of every part , maketh increase of the body unto the edifying of itself in love.
corruption_summary: Church unity is pursued either by doctrinal indifference or abandoned altogether for private religion — where the tabernacle shows a unity that is designed, specified, fastened, and costly.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption runs to two extremes, and the couplings rebuke both. On one side is the unity that is purchased by subtraction, in which the loops are loosened and the taches thrown away so that anyone may be joined to anything, and the resulting fabric is one only in the sense that a heap is one. Scripture’s unity is nothing like that: fifty loops must answer fifty loops exactly, blue to blue, edge to edge, or the curtains do not meet. On the other side is the private Christianity that treats the seam as optional, holding that a man may be joined to Christ while joined to no congregation — a curtain persuaded it is a tabernacle. Exodus counts the loops precisely because a dwelling is not a collection of hangings.

Recover the plain sense: unity is a designed thing, specified by God, and it is fastened at cost — taches of gold for the inner curtains, taches of brass for the outer. The refrain that it may be one is the point of the whole chapter, and it culminates in our Lord’s prayer that they all may be one. Then take Eph 4:16 as the working principle: the body is compacted by that which every joint supplieth, which means the seams are where the labour is. Congregational life is largely the maintenance of couplings — bearing with one another, forgiving, keeping the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace — and a fabric always tears at the seam, which is precisely why the loops were counted.
roots_summary: Latin copula, a bond — the seam joining curtain to curtain, until the refrain is answered: that it may be one.
roots_lines: Coupling — Latin copula, a tie; Old French copler, to join.
In Exodus, the seam where two sets of curtains are united.
Fifty loops answering fifty loops, fastened by taches of gold and of brass.
The refrain of Exo 26 is that it may be one (vv. 6, 11).
Eph 4:16: the body compacted by that which every joint supplieth.
usage: The loops must answer exactly — unity by specification, not by subtraction.
Gold taches within, brass without: the joining is costly at every layer.
A fabric tears at the seam, which is why the couplings are counted.
